tasks.title: Clearance plot — read the axes
tasks.context: The figure shows a **solid brown parabola** $g$ and a **dashed green line** $f$. No formulas are printed. Reason from the ticks, crossings, and relative heights only. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solid curve meets the horizontal axis at exactly two points.
The turning point of the solid curve lies below the dashed line.
The two graphs meet at exactly one real point.
On the open interval between the solid curve's two axis crossings, the solid curve stays below the dashed line.
The solid curve opens downwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A parabola meets the horizontal axis wherever its height is zero, which on the figure is every brown crossing of that axis.

Two distinct crossings are marked, one on each side of the origin.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

$$-x^{2}+4=0$$

$$x=\pm 2$$

Two crossings are visible and the hidden rule confirms the count, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The turning point is the unique marked peak on the solid curve, sitting on the vertical axis.

At that common abscissa the brown mark sits strictly above the green line.

$$g(0)=4$$

$$f(0)=2$$

$$4>2$$

The turning point lies above the dashed line, not below it, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The two traces meet where they share a height, so count the brown–green crossings.

The figure shows one crossing left of the origin and one on the positive side.

$$g(x)-f(x)=-x^{2}+x+2$$

$$-x^{2}+x+2=-(x-2)(x+1)$$

$$x=-1,\; x$$

$$-1,\; x=2$$

Two meetings are visible, not one, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Between the two brown axis crossings the solid curve arches above the axis while the dashed line cuts through lower heights.

Comparing the traces on that interval, brown stays above green.

$$g(0)=4$$

$$f(0)=2$$

$$4>2$$

The solid curve is above the dashed line there, not below it, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Whether a parabola opens downwards is read from the arms falling away from a peak.

The solid curve has exactly that shape: a peak on the vertical axis and arms sloping down to the two crossings.

$$a=-1$$

$$a<0$$

The opening is downwards, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Hidden models:

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4\qquad f(x)=-x+2$$

Vertex $(0,4)$; roots $\pm 2$; meetings at $x=-1$ and $x=2$. Read crossings, the peak, and relative heights from the figure; the algebra only checks the reading.

tasks.title: Discrete samples — diagnose the degree
tasks.context: A sequence $s_n$ is recorded in the table for $n=0,1,2,3,4,5$. No closed form is supplied. Decide each claim from the table alone. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of $s_n$ are constant.
The second differences of $s_n$ are constant and equal to $2$.
A single linear rule fits every listed point.
Rebuilding a quadratic $an^{2}+bn+c$ from the second-difference constant recovers the leading coefficient $a=1$.
The listed heights satisfy $s_0=s_4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

First differences are the neighbouring gaps in the $s$-row, which the table does not print: they have to be formed by hand.

$$s_{1}-s_{0}=0-3$$

$$0-3=-3$$

$$s_{2}-s_{1}=-1-0$$

$$-1-0=-1$$

$$(-3,-1,1,3,5)$$

These gaps change from step to step, so they are not constant, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Second differences are the gaps of that first-difference row.

$$(-1)-(-3)=2$$

$$1-(-1)=2$$

$$3-1=2$$

$$5-3=2$$

$$(2,2,2,2)$$

Every second difference equals $2$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A linear model forces constant first differences. Here the first differences move while the second ones stand still — the signature of a quadratic, not a line.

$$2a=2$$

$$a=1\neq 0$$

No single line can fit every listed point, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

For unit spacing, a quadratic sequence has constant second difference $2a$.

$$2a=2$$

$$a=1$$

The rebuilt leading coefficient is $1$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Read the two table entries directly, without rebuilding anything.

$$s_{0}=3$$

$$s_{4}=3$$

The two heights agree, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Hidden model:

$$s_n=n^{2}-4n+3$$

Second differences constantly $2$, so $a=1$; the table is symmetric about $n=2$.

tasks.title: Ticket desk — revenue table
tasks.context: A club sells tickets at price $p$ euros. The table records total revenue $R$ (in euros) observed at five prices. No formula is printed on the desk sheet. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Among the listed prices, revenue is largest at $p=4$.
Revenue at $p=3$ equals revenue at $p=5$.
Revenue increases at every step from $p=1$ to $p=5$.
The revenue at $p=2$ is $12$ euros.
Raising the price from $4$ to $5$ decreases the listed revenue.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

List the five recorded revenues in price order and pick out the largest.

$$(7,12,15,16,15)$$

$$16$$

The unique maximum is $16$, sitting at $p=4$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The two named prices are different columns of the same row.

$$R(3)=15$$

$$R(5)=15$$

The two revenues match, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An always-increasing sequence would have every step strictly positive.

$$R(4)=16$$

$$R(5)=15$$

$$15-16=-1$$

The sequence falls on the last step, so it is not increasing throughout, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The column headed $p=2$ holds the recorded revenue at that price.

$$R(2)=12$$

$$12$$

The listed revenue is $12$ euros, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A price increase from $4$ to $5$ changes revenue by the difference of those two entries.

$$R(4)=16$$

$$R(5)=15$$

$$R(5)-R(4)=15-16$$

$$15-16=-1$$

Revenue falls when the price is raised from $4$ to $5$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Hidden model $R(p)=p(8-p)$. Students need only the table: the unique listed peak is $16$ at $p=4$, and the row is symmetric about that price.

tasks.title: Line and parabola — intersection algebra
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=2x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-3x+1$. Work in symbols; no figure is supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs meet at exactly two real points.
The axis of $g$ is $x=\frac{3}{2}$.
The vertex height of $g$ equals $-\frac{5}{4}$.
The product of the roots of $g$ equals $1$.
There exist real numbers $A,B,C$ such that $g(x)=A\,f(x)^2+B\,f(x)+C$; one such triple is $A=\frac{1}{4}$, $B=-2$, $C=\frac{11}{4}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings of a line and a parabola are the real zeros of their difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x+1-(2x+1)$$

$$x^{2}-3x+1-(2x+1)=x^{2}-5x$$

$$x(x-5)=0$$

$$x=0,\; x$$

$$0,\; x=5$$

Two distinct real roots give two meetings, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ is the vertical line through $-b/(2a)$.

$$a=1$$

$$b=-3$$

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$-\frac{-3}{2\cdot 1}=\frac{3}{2}$$

The axis is $x=\frac{3}{2}$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertex height is the value of $g$ on its axis.

$$g\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}-3\cdot\frac{3}{2}+1$$

$$\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+1=-\frac{5}{4}$$

The vertex height is $-\frac{5}{4}$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Vieta reads the product of the roots from the constant term over the leading coefficient, without solving.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$\frac{c}{a}=\frac{1}{1}$$

$$\frac{1}{1}=1$$

The product is $1$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A line with nonzero slope already produces an $x^{2}$ term once it is squared, so $f^{2}$, $f$ and $1$ span every parabola.

$$f(x)^{2}=(2x+1)^{2}$$

$$(2x+1)^{2}=4x^{2}+4x+1$$

$$A=\frac{1}{4}$$

$$B=-2$$

$$C=\frac{11}{4}$$

$$\frac{1}{4}(2x+1)^2-2(2x+1)+\frac{11}{4}=x^2-3x+1$$

The named triple reproduces $g$ exactly, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$f(x)=2x+1\qquad g(x)=x^{2}-3x+1$$

Meetings at $x=0$ and $x=5$; axis $x=\frac{3}{2}$; vertex height $-\frac{5}{4}$; rewrite $A=\frac{1}{4}$, $B=-2$, $C=\frac{11}{4}$.

tasks.title: Sliding slope family
tasks.context: For each real $t$ let $f_t(x)=tx$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+1$. Study how the line family meets the fixed parabola. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For $t=0$ the graphs share no real point.
The graphs never miss each other: every real $t$ produces at least one meeting.
Tangency occurs for exactly one real value of $t$.
When $t=3$ the graphs miss each other.
The axis of $g$ depends on $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For $t=0$ the line is the horizontal axis, so meetings solve $x^{2}+1=0$.

$$g(x)-f_0(x)=x^{2}+1$$

$$x^{2}+1=0$$

No real solution exists, so the graphs share no real point, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The discriminant of the difference is a quadratic in the slope parameter.

$$g-f_t=x^{2}-tx+1$$

$$\Delta=t^{2}-4$$

$$|t|<2$$

$$\Delta<0$$

The graphs miss whenever $|t|<2$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Tangency is the boundary $\Delta=0$.

$$t^{2}-4=0$$

$$t=\pm 2$$

Exactly two tangent slopes exist, not one, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Substitute the named slope into the same discriminant.

$$t=3$$

$$\Delta=9-4=5>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two meetings, not a miss, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The axis of $g$ is computed from $g$ alone.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+1$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2}$$

$$-\frac{0}{2}=0$$

The axis stays $x=0$ for every $t$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)-f_t(x)=x^{2}-tx+1\qquad\Delta=t^{2}-4$$

Miss when $|t|<2$, tangency at $t=\pm 2$, two meetings when $|t|>2$.

tasks.title: Rebuild from vertex and a point
tasks.context: A parabola has vertex $(2,-3)$ and passes through $(0,5)$. It opens upwards. Rebuild its rule and test the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$.
The $y$-intercept equals $5$.
The axis of symmetry is $x=2$.
The vertex lies above the horizontal axis.
At $x=4$ one has $g(4)=-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Vertex form with the given turning point is $g(x)=a(x-2)^{2}-3$. Passing through $(0,5)$ fixes $a$.

$$g(0)=a(0-2)^{2}-3$$

$$a(0-2)^{2}-3=5$$

$$4a-3=5$$

$$a=2$$

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

The rebuilt rule matches the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Passing through $(0,5)$ is exactly the claim that the graph meets the vertical axis at height $5$.

$$g(0)=2(0-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(0)=5$$

The $y$-intercept is $5$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The axis is the vertical line through the vertex.

$$x=2$$

$$g(2)=-3$$

The axis is $x=2$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The vertex height is the number named in the stem.

$$g(2)=-3$$

$$-3<0$$

The vertex lies strictly below the horizontal axis, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The point $x=4$ is as far to the right of the axis as $x=0$ is to the left, so the heights agree.

$$g(4)=2(4-2)^{2}-3$$

$$2(4-2)^{2}-3=8-3$$

$$8-3=5$$

$$5\neq -3$$

The height at $x=4$ is $5$, not $-3$, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Nesting a line inside a parabola
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$. Study the nested rules $g(f(x))$ and $f(g(x))$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The nested rule $g(f(x))$ expands to $x^{2}+2x+1$.
The nested rule $f(g(x))$ expands to $x^{2}+1$.
The two nested rules are identical as functions.
At $x=1$ one has $g(f(1))=f(g(1))$.
The highest power in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Substitute the line into the parabola and expand.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$(x+1)^{2}=x^{2}+2x+1$$

The expansion matches, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The other order feeds the parabola into the line.

$$f(g(x))=f(x^{2})$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

The expansion matches, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The two expansions already differ by the middle term $2x$.

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

The nested rules are not identical, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Evaluate each nested rule at the named input.

$$f(1)=2$$

$$g(f(1))=4$$

$$g(1)=1$$

$$f(g(1))=2$$

$$4\neq 2$$

The two nested values differ at $x=1$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

After expansion $f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$ is still quadratic.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

$$x^{2}$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Composition of a line and a parabola stays quadratic; order matters.

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1\qquad f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

tasks.title: Factored parabola — Vieta reads
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=2(x-1)(x-4)$. Decide each claim without expanding first if you can. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots are $1$ and $4$.
The axis is $x=\frac{5}{2}$.
Expanded, the middle coefficient equals $-10$.
The constant term equals $8$.
The vertex height equals $-4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product $2(x-1)(x-4)$ vanishes precisely where a factor vanishes.

$$x-1=0$$

$$x-4=0$$

$$x=1,\; x$$

$$1,\; x=4$$

The roots are $1$ and $4$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis bisects the two roots.

$$x=\frac{1+4}{2}$$

$$\frac{1+4}{2}=\frac{5}{2}$$

The axis is $x=\frac{5}{2}$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Expand the product, then distribute the leading $2$.

$$(x-1)(x-4)=x^{2}-5x+4$$

$$2(x^{2}-5x+4)=2x^{2}-10x+8$$

The middle coefficient is $-10$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The constant term is the value at the origin, or the last term after the expansion above.

$$g(0)=2(-1)(-4)$$

$$2(-1)(-4)=8$$

The constant term is $8$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Evaluate the factored form on the axis.

$$g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=2\left(\frac{5}{2}-1\right)\left(\frac{5}{2}-4\right)$$

$$2\cdot\frac{3}{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{2}$$

$$-\frac{9}{2}\neq -4$$

The vertex height is $-\frac{9}{2}$, not $-4$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=2x^{2}-10x+8$$

Roots $1$ and $4$; axis $x=\frac{5}{2}$; vertex height $-\frac{9}{2}$.

tasks.title: Figure for g, table for a line
tasks.context: The figure shows an unknown parabola $g$ (solid brown; no formula). Separately, the table lists an unknown line $\ell$ at four inputs. Use the figure for claims about $g$ and the table for claims about $\ell$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solid curve crosses the horizontal axis twice.
The solid curve's turning point lies below the horizontal axis.
The tabled rule has constant first difference $2$.
The tabled rule is consistent with slope $2$.
At $x=0$ the tabled height equals $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Count the brown meetings with the horizontal axis on the figure.

Two crossings appear, symmetric about the origin.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$x^{2}-4=0$$

$$x=\pm 2$$

Two axis crossings are visible, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The marked trough sits below the axis on the vertical scale.

$$g(0)=-4$$

$$-4<0$$

The turning point lies below the horizontal axis, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Form neighbouring gaps of the $y$-row; the table does not print them.

$$3-1=2$$

$$5-3=2$$

$$7-5=2$$

$$(2,2,2)$$

The constant gap is $2$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

For unit spacing, a constant first difference is exactly the slope of the line.

$$m=2$$

$$2$$

The table is consistent with slope $2$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Read the table entry under $x=0$.

$$\ell(0)=1$$

$$1$$

The tabled height is $1$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=x^{2}-4\qquad \ell(x)=2x+1$$

Trough $(0,-4)$; roots $\pm 2$; the table is an arithmetic sequence of step $2$.

tasks.title: Dense clearance brief
tasks.context: A dock crane's clearance is modelled by a parabola $g$ that opens downwards, turns at $(1,5)$, and meets the deck $y=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x=3$. A linear sensor path $f$ passes through $(0,2)$ with slope $-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule for $g$ is $g(x)=-(x+1)(x-3)$.
The unscaled product $-(x+1)(x-3)$ already has vertex height $5$.
The sensor path is $f(x)=-x+3$.
The sensor path and the clearance curve meet at exactly one real point.
At $x=1$ the sensor lies below the clearance peak.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Opening downwards with those roots means $g(x)=k(x+1)(x-3)$ for some $k<0$. The unscaled choice $k=-1$ must still hit height $5$ at $x=1$.

$$-(1+1)(1-3)=-(2)(-2)$$

$$-(2)(-2)=4$$

$$4\neq 5$$

The unscaled factorisation misses the named vertex height, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The same evaluation as in A is the vertex height of the unscaled product.

$$-(x+1)(x-3)\big|_{x=1}$$

$$1}=4$$

$$4\neq 5$$

The unscaled vertex height is $4$, not $5$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Slope $-1$ through $(0,2)$ is point-slope with intercept $2$.

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

$$-x+2\neq -x+3$$

The intercept is $2$, not $3$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Scale so that $g(1)=5$: $k(2)(-2)=5$ forces $k=-\frac{5}{4}$. Then form $g-f$.

$$g(x)=-\frac{5}{4}(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$-\frac{5}{4}(x+1)(x-3)=-\frac{5}{4}x^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x+\frac{15}{4}$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-\frac{5}{4}x^{2}+\frac{7}{2}x+\frac{7}{4}$$

$$\Delta=\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^{2}-4\left(-\frac{5}{4}\right)\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)=\frac{21}{1}>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two meetings, not one, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

At the peak abscissa compare the sensor height with the named vertex height $5$.

$$f(1)=-1+2$$

$$-1+2=1$$

$$1<5$$

The sensor lies below the clearance peak, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Vertex $(1,5)$ with roots $-1$ and $3$ forces the stretch $-\frac{5}{4}$.

$$g(x)=-\frac{5}{4}(x+1)(x-3)\qquad f(x)=-x+2$$

The difference has positive discriminant, so two meetings.

tasks.title: Trough touching a level line
tasks.context: A **solid brown parabola** $g$ and a **dashed green horizontal line** appear on the axes. Formulas are withheld. Decide each claim from the figure alone. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solid curve has a lowest point (not a highest point).
The solid curve crosses the horizontal axis twice.
The dashed line lies entirely above the solid curve.
The solid curve and the dashed line meet at exactly two points.
The solid curve opens upwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Arms that rise on both sides of a marked trough mean the solid curve opens upwards, so the marked turn is a minimum.

The figure shows exactly that trough between the two axis crossings.

$$a=1$$

$$a>0$$

The turning point is a lowest point, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Count where brown meets the horizontal axis.

Two distinct crossings are marked, both on the positive side of the origin.

$$(x-1)(x-3)=0$$

$$x=1,\; x$$

$$1,\; x=3$$

Two crossings appear, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Outside the roots an upward-opening parabola climbs without bound, so it eventually rises above any fixed horizontal line.

On the figure the arms already sit above the dashed line near the window edges.

$$g(0)=3>-1$$

$$g(4)=3>-1$$

The dashed line is not entirely above the solid curve, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The dashed level cuts the trough at its lowest point and nowhere else: a tangency, not a pair of crossings.

$$g(x)+1=x^{2}-4x+4$$

$$x^{2}-4x+4=(x-2)^{2}$$

$$(x-2)^{2}=0$$

$$x=2$$

There is exactly one shared point, not two, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A trough between rising arms is the signature of an upward-opening parabola.

That is the shape of the solid curve on the figure.

$$a=1$$

$$a>0$$

The solid curve opens upwards, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+3\qquad y=-1$$

Vertex $(2,-1)$; the level is tangent at the trough; roots $1$ and $3$.

tasks.title: Evenly spaced line samples
tasks.context: The table lists values of an unknown rule $y(x)$ at five equally spaced inputs. No formula is printed. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-row are constant.
The constant first difference equals $2$.
The rule is consistent with a line of slope $3$.
Extending the pattern one step gives $y(5)=14$.
The second differences of the $y$-row all vanish.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Form neighbouring gaps of the $y$-row.

$$2-(-1)=3$$

$$5-2=3$$

$$8-5=3$$

$$11-8=3$$

$$(3,3,3,3)$$

Every gap equals $3$, so the first differences are constant, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The constant gap just computed is $3$, not $2$.

$$\Delta^{(1)}=3$$

$$3\neq 2$$

The constant first difference is $3$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For unit spacing, a constant first difference is exactly the slope of the line.

$$m=3$$

$$3$$

Slope $3$ matches the claim, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

One more step of size $3$ continues the arithmetic sequence.

$$y(5)=y(4)+3$$

$$y(4)+3=11+3$$

$$11+3=14$$

The extrapolated value is $14$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Second differences of a line with constant first differences are all zero.

$$3-3=0$$

$$3-3=0$$

$$3-3=0$$

$$(0,0,0)$$

The second differences all vanish, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$y=3x-1$$

Constant first difference $3$; the next term is $14$.

tasks.title: Ball toss — height against time
tasks.context: A ball is tossed straight up. The figure shows height $h$ (metres) against time $t$ (seconds) as a **solid brown** curve; the horizontal axis is ground level. No formula is printed. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The ball is at ground level at exactly two times visible on the figure.
The greatest height occurs at $t=2$.
At $t=1$ the height is greater than at $t=5$.
After the peak, height keeps rising.
The greatest height on the figure is $8$ metres.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Ground meetings are brown crossings of the horizontal axis.

Two crossings appear, near the origin and far to the right.

$$h(t)=-t^{2}+6t$$

$$-t^{2}+6t=t(6-t)$$

$$t(6-t)=0$$

$$t=0,\; t$$

$$0,\; t=6$$

Exactly two ground times are visible, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The peak is the marked turning point. Its abscissa on the time axis is $t=3$, midway between the two ground crossings.

$$t=-\frac{6}{2(-1)}$$

$$-\frac{6}{2(-1)}=3$$

$$3\neq 2$$

The greatest height occurs at $t=3$, not at $t=2$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The curve is symmetric about $t=3$, so heights equally far from the peak agree.

$$h(1)=5$$

$$h(5)=5$$

The heights are equal, not strictly greater, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Past the peak the solid curve slopes down toward the second ground crossing.

$$h(3)=9$$

$$h(4)=8$$

$$8<9$$

Height falls after the peak, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Read the peak height on the vertical scale.

$$h(3)=-9+18$$

$$-9+18=9$$

$$9\neq 8$$

The greatest height is $9$ metres, not $8$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$h(t)=-t^{2}+6t$$

Peak $(3,9)$; ground times $t=0$ and $t=6$.

tasks.title: Completing the square with small coeffs
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=x^{2}+6x+5$. Decide each claim. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: In vertex form, $g(x)=(x+3)^{2}-4$.
The vertex is $(-3,-4)$.
Both roots are positive.
The discriminant equals $15$.
Shifting the graph up by $5$ units produces a perfect square with a double root.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Complete the square by taking half the middle coefficient.

$$x^{2}+6x+5=(x^{2}+6x+9)-9+5$$

$$(x+3)^{2}-4$$

The vertex form matches, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

From the vertex form the turn is at $x=-3$ with height $-4$.

$$x=-3$$

$$g(-3)=-4$$

The vertex is $(-3,-4)$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Factor the completed square, or read the constant and middle coefficients via Vieta.

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x+5)$$

$$x=-1,\; x$$

$$-1,\; x=-5$$

Both roots are negative, not positive, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The discriminant is $b^{2}-4ac$.

$$\Delta=6^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 5$$

$$6^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 5=36-20$$

$$36-20=16$$

$$16\neq 15$$

The discriminant is $16$, not $15$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A vertical shift of $4$, not $5$, cancels the constant in vertex form.

$$g(x)+4=(x+3)^{2}$$

$$g(x)+5=(x+3)^{2}+1$$

Shifting up by $5$ leaves a leftover $+1$, not a perfect square, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Vertical shift of a parabola
tasks.context: Let $g_s(x)=x^{2}-4x+s$ for a real shift $s$, and let $f(x)=0$ be the horizontal axis. Track how $s$ changes the meetings with the axis. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For $s=3$ the graph of $g_s$ meets the axis twice.
For $s=4$ the graph of $g_s$ touches the axis exactly once.
For $s=5$ the graph of $g_s$ misses the axis.
The axis of symmetry of $g_s$ is $x=2$ for every $s$.
The vertex height of $g_s$ equals $s-4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings with the axis are the roots of $g_s$. Their count follows the discriminant.

$$\Delta=16-4s$$

$$s=3$$

$$\Delta=4>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two real roots, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Tangency with the axis is the boundary $\Delta=0$.

$$s=4$$

$$\Delta=0$$

$$g_4(x)=(x-2)^{2}$$

A repeated root means a single touch, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A negative discriminant means no real root.

$$s=5$$

$$\Delta=-4<0$$

The graph misses the axis, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The axis $-b/(2a)$ uses only the $x^{2}$ and $x$ coefficients, which do not involve $s$.

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$-\frac{-4}{2\cdot 1}=2$$

The axis stays $x=2$ for every $s$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Evaluate on that fixed axis.

$$g_s(2)=4-8+s$$

$$4-8+s=s-4$$

The vertex height is $s-4$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g_s(x)=x^{2}-4x+s\qquad\Delta=16-4s$$

Axis $x=2$ for every $s$; vertex height $s-4$.

tasks.title: Rebuild a line from two points
tasks.context: A line passes through $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$. Rebuild it and test the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The slope equals $-2$.
The rule is $f(x)=-2x+4$.
The line meets the horizontal axis at $x=2$.
At $x=1$ the height equals $1$.
The line falls from left to right.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Slope is rise over run between the two given points.

$$m=\frac{0-4}{2-0}$$

$$\frac{0-4}{2-0}=\frac{-4}{2}$$

$$\frac{-4}{2}=-2$$

The slope is $-2$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Point-slope with intercept $4$ and slope $-2$ is already slope-intercept form.

$$f(x)=-2x+4$$

$$f(0)=4$$

The rebuilt rule matches, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The given point $(2,0)$ is exactly a meeting with the horizontal axis.

$$f(2)=-4+4$$

$$f(2)=0$$

The horizontal-axis meeting is at $x=2$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Evaluate the rebuilt rule at the midpoint of the two given abscissas.

$$f(1)=-2+4$$

$$-2+4=2$$

$$2\neq 1$$

The height is $2$, not $1$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A negative slope means the line falls from left to right.

$$m=-2$$

$$m<0$$

The line falls from left to right, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$f(x)=-2x+4$$

Slope $-2$; intercepts $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$.

tasks.title: Line outside a shifted parabola
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=2x-1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-4$. Compare $f(g(x))$ with $g(f(x))$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The nested rule $f(g(x))$ equals $2x^{2}-9$.
The nested rule $g(f(x))$ equals $4x^{2}-4x-3$.
Both nested rules have the same highest power of $x$.
The nested rule $f(g(x))$ has a linear term in $x$.
At $x=0$ one has $f(g(0))=g(f(0))$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Feed the parabola into the line.

$$f(g(x))=2(x^{2}-4)-1$$

$$2x^{2}-8-1=2x^{2}-9$$

The expansion matches, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The other order squares the line first.

$$g(f(x))=(2x-1)^{2}-4$$

$$4x^{2}-4x+1-4=4x^{2}-4x-3$$

The expansion matches, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Both expansions are quadratic: the highest power in each is $x^{2}$.

$$2x^{2}-9$$

$$4x^{2}-4x-3$$

The highest powers agree, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A linear term would be a multiple of $x^{1}$.

$$f(g(x))=2x^{2}-9$$

$$2x^{2}-9$$

The rule $2x^{2}-9$ has no $x$ term, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Evaluate each nested rule at the origin.

$$f(g(0))=f(-4)$$

$$f(-4)=-9$$

$$g(f(0))=g(-1)$$

$$g(-1)=-3$$

$$-9\neq -3$$

The two values differ, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Order of nesting changes coefficients even when the highest power matches.

$$f(g(x))=2x^{2}-9\qquad g(f(x))=4x^{2}-4x-3$$

tasks.title: Opposite roots
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=(x+3)(x-3)$. Decide each claim. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis of symmetry is the vertical coordinate axis.
The function $g$ is odd: $g(-x)=-g(x)$ for every $x$.
Both roots are positive.
The vertex is $(0,9)$.
For every $x$ one has $g(x)\ge 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Roots $\pm 3$ are symmetric about the origin, so the axis is the vertical coordinate axis.

$$x=\frac{-3+3}{2}$$

$$\frac{-3+3}{2}=0$$

The axis is $x=0$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Oddness requires $g(-x)=-g(x)$. Expand first.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-9$$

$$g(-x)=x^{2}-9$$

$$x^{2}-9=g(x)$$

$$g(x)\neq -g(x)$$

$g$ is even, not odd, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Read the roots from the factors.

$$x=-3,\; x$$

$$-3,\; x=3$$

One root is negative, so not both are positive, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The turn on the axis $x=0$ has height $g(0)$.

$$g(0)=-9$$

$$(0,-9)\neq(0,9)$$

The vertex is $(0,-9)$, not $(0,9)$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

An upward-opening parabola is bounded below by its vertex height, which here is negative.

$$g(0)=-9$$

$$-9<0$$

$g$ takes negative values, so it is not always at least $0$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=x^{2}-9$$

Even; vertex $(0,-9)$; roots $\pm 3$.

tasks.title: Peak over a level, plus a line table
tasks.context: The figure shows a solid brown parabola and a dashed green horizontal line; no formulas are printed on the sketch. Separately, the table lists an unknown line at four inputs. Use the figure for the curve claims and the table for the line claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solid curve has a highest point (not a trough).
The solid curve crosses the horizontal axis twice.
The dashed line lies above the peak of the solid curve.
The tabled rule has constant first difference $3$.
The tabled rule is consistent with slope $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A marked peak with arms falling on both sides means a maximum.

$$a=-1$$

$$a<0$$

The solid curve has a highest point, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Two axis crossings of brown are visible, both on the positive side of the origin.

$$(x-1)(x-5)=0$$

$$x=1$$

$$x=5$$

Two crossings appear, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The peak sits above the dashed level on the figure. Read both heights at the trough's abscissa.

$$g(3)=4$$

$$4>1$$

The dashed line is not above the peak, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Form neighbouring gaps of the tabled row; the table does not print them.

$$1-4=-3$$

$$-2-1=-3$$

$$-5-(-2)=-3$$

$$(-3,-3,-3)$$

$$-3\neq 3$$

The constant first difference is $-3$, not $3$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

For unit spacing the slope equals that constant first difference.

$$m=-3$$

$$-3\neq 3$$

The table is consistent with slope $-3$, not $3$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=-(x-1)(x-5)\qquad y=1\qquad \ell(x)=-3x+4$$

Peak $(3,4)$; the level cuts the hill twice; the table has step $-3$.

tasks.title: Market brief in prose
tasks.context: Weekend ticket price $p$ euros yields revenue $R(p)=p(16-p)$. Staff cost for the same price experiment is logged as the line $C(p)=2p+20$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Revenue is a downward-opening parabola in $p$.
Revenue is largest at $p=8$.
Profit $R-C$ is largest at $p=7$.
At $p=0$ revenue is less than cost.
At $p=10$ revenue exceeds cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand the revenue rule and read the leading coefficient.

$$R(p)=16p-p^{2}$$

$$a=-1$$

$$a<0$$

Revenue opens downwards, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis of a downward-opening parabola is the unique maximiser.

$$p=-\frac{16}{2(-1)}$$

$$-\frac{16}{2(-1)}=8$$

Revenue is largest at $p=8$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Profit is a different parabola; its own axis is the profit maximiser.

$$\Pi(p)=R(p)-C(p)$$

$$R(p)-C(p)=-p^{2}+14p-20$$

$$p=-\frac{14}{2(-1)}$$

$$-\frac{14}{2(-1)}=7$$

Profit is largest at $p=7$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluate both rules at the origin.

$$R(0)=0$$

$$C(0)=20$$

$$0<20$$

Revenue is less than cost at $p=0$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Evaluate both rules at the named price.

$$R(10)=10\cdot 6$$

$$10\cdot 6=60$$

$$C(10)=20+20$$

$$20+20=40$$

$$60>40$$

Revenue exceeds cost at $p=10$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$R(p)=p(16-p)\qquad C(p)=2p+20\qquad\Pi(p)=-p^{2}+14p-20$$

Revenue peaks at $p=8$; profit peaks at $p=7$.

tasks.title: Parabola against a submerged level
tasks.context: The figure shows a **solid brown parabola** and a **dashed green horizontal line**. No closed forms are printed. Work from ticks and marked turns only. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solid curve crosses the horizontal axis once on each side of the origin.
The dashed line sits at height $0$.
The solid curve and the dashed line share exactly two points.
The turning point of the solid curve lies below the dashed line.
The solid curve opens upwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Brown meets the horizontal axis once left of zero and once right of zero.

$$x^{2}-4=0$$

$$x=\pm 2$$

One crossing on each side of the origin is visible, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The dashed line is the green horizontal trace. Reading its height on the vertical scale places it at $-2$, not at $0$.

Height $0$ would be the axis itself; the dashed line is strictly below it.

$$y=-2$$

$$-2\neq 0$$

The dashed line is not at height $0$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Brown dips to its trough and climbs again; the dashed level cuts both sides of the trough.

$$x^{2}-4=-2$$

$$x^{2}=2$$

$$x=\pm\sqrt{2}$$

Exactly two shared points are visible, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The trough of the solid curve sits below the dashed line: the lowest brown mark is lower than the green level.

$$g(0)=-4$$

$$-4<-2$$

The turning point lies below the dashed line, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A trough between rising arms is the signature of an upward-opening parabola.

$$a=1$$

$$a>0$$

The solid curve opens upwards, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=x^{2}-4\qquad y=-2$$

Vertex $(0,-4)$; roots $\pm 2$; the level $y=-2$ cuts the trough twice.

tasks.title: Quadratic growth in a table
tasks.context: An unknown function $h$ is sampled at $x=0,1,2,3,4,5$ in the table. No algebraic expression is given. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences are constant.
The second differences are constant and equal to $4$.
A linear model can fit every listed point.
Extending the second-difference pattern gives $h(6)=20$.
The second differences of the listed heights are constant.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Form neighbouring gaps of the $h$-row.

$$(-1)-0=-1$$

$$0-(-1)=1$$

$$3-0=3$$

$$(-1,1,3,5,7)$$

These gaps increase, so they are not constant, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Second differences are the gaps of that first-difference row.

$$1-(-1)=2$$

$$3-1=2$$

$$5-3=2$$

$$7-5=2$$

$$(2,2,2,2)$$

$$2\neq 4$$

The constant second difference is $2$, not $4$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A line would need constant first differences. Here the first differences move, so no single line fits all six points.

$$2a=2$$

$$a=1\neq 0$$

A linear model fails, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

One more constant second difference $2$ lifts the last first difference from $7$ to $9$.

$$h(6)=h(5)+9$$

$$h(5)+9=15+9$$

$$15+9=24$$

$$24\neq 20$$

The extrapolated value is $24$, not $20$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The second-difference row computed above is $(2,2,2,2)$.

$$(2,2,2,2)$$

$$2a=2$$

The second differences are constant, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$h(x)=x^{2}-2x$$

Second differences constantly $2$; $h(6)=24$.

tasks.title: Workshop cost log
tasks.context: A workshop logs total cost $C$ (euros) against daily batch size $q$ in the table. No cost formula is written in the logbook. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Among the listed batches, cost is smallest at $q=2$.
Cost at $q=0$ equals cost at $q=4$.
Cost rises from $q=2$ to $q=3$.
The second differences of the cost row are constant.
Raising the batch from $4$ to $5$ increases cost by $5$ euros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compare the six cost entries.

$$(9,6,5,6,9,14)$$

$$\min=5$$

The unique listed minimum sits at $q=2$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Read the two columns $q=0$ and $q=4$.

$$C(0)=9$$

$$C(4)=9$$

The two costs match, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Compare the neighbouring entries at $q=2$ and $q=3$.

$$C(2)=5$$

$$C(3)=6$$

$$6-5=1$$

Cost rises from $q=2$ to $q=3$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Form first differences, then their gaps. The table does not print either row.

$$(-3,-1,1,3,5)$$

$$(2,2,2,2)$$

Second differences are constant, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Subtract the neighbouring listed costs.

$$C(5)-C(4)=14-9$$

$$14-9=5$$

The increase is $5$ euros, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$C(q)=q^{2}-4q+9$$

Listed minimum $5$ at $q=2$; second differences constantly $2$.

tasks.title: Signed gap and tangency test
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=4x-1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+x-1$. Decide each claim. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The discriminant of $g-f$ is positive.
The graphs are tangent for this pair.
The axis of $g$ is $x=-\frac{1}{2}$.
At $x=0$ one has $g(0)=f(0)$.
The leading coefficient of $g-f$ equals $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Form the difference and compute $b^{2}-4ac$.

$$g-f=x^{2}+x-1-(4x-1)$$

$$x^{2}+x-1-(4x-1)=x^{2}-3x$$

$$\Delta=(-3)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 0=9>0$$

The discriminant is positive, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Tangency needs a repeated root, hence $\Delta=0$.

$$\Delta=9>0$$

$$x(x-3)=0$$

$$x=0,\; x$$

$$0,\; x=3$$

The graphs cross twice rather than touch, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The axis uses only the coefficients of $g$.

$$x=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

The axis is $x=-\frac{1}{2}$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluate both rules at the origin.

$$g(0)=-1$$

$$f(0)=-1$$

The values agree at the origin, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The leading coefficient of $g-f=x^{2}-3x$ is the factor in front of $x^{2}$.

$$a=1$$

$$1\neq 2$$

The leading coefficient is $1$, not $2$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x\qquad\Delta=9$$

Two meetings, at $x=0$ and $x=3$; axis of $g$ is $x=-\frac{1}{2}$.

tasks.title: Leading coefficient family
tasks.context: Let $g_a(x)=a x^{2}-4x+3$ with $a\neq 0$, and let $f(x)=3$. Watch how the leading coefficient changes meetings with the level $y=3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $a\neq 0$ the graphs meet at $x=0$.
When $a=1$ there is a second meeting at $x=4$.
When $a=2$ the second meeting is at $x=3$.
The axis of $g_a$ is independent of $a$.
If $a=-1$, then $g_a$ opens upwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The shared intercept is always a meeting, because the constant term of $g_a$ equals the level.

$$g_a(0)=3$$

$$3=f(0)$$

The graphs meet at $x=0$ for every $a\neq 0$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The remaining meetings solve $g_a(x)=3$.

$$a=1:\quad x^{2}-4x$$

$$1:\quad x^{2}-4x=0$$

$$x(x-4)=0$$

The second root is $x=4$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Repeat the same difference with $a=2$.

$$2x^{2}-4x=0$$

$$2x(x-2)=0$$

$$x=2\neq 3$$

The second meeting is at $x=2$, not $x=3$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The axis $-b/(2a)$ still involves the leading coefficient.

$$x=\frac{4}{2a}$$

$$\frac{4}{2a}=\frac{2}{a}$$

The axis slides with $a$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The opening is the sign of the leading coefficient.

$$a=-1$$

$$a<0$$

The parabola opens downwards, not upwards, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g_a(x)-3=ax^{2}-4x$$

Always a meeting at $x=0$; the other meeting is at $x=4/a$; axis $x=2/a$.

tasks.title: Rebuild from roots and leading coefficient
tasks.context: A monic parabola has roots $x=-1$ and $x=3$. Rebuild $g$ and test the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $g(x)=(x+1)(x-3)$.
Expanded, $g(x)=x^{2}-2x+3$.
The axis is $x=0$.
The vertex height equals $-3$.
The constant term equals $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Monic with those roots means the product of the two linear factors, with leading coefficient $1$.

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$g(x)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

The rebuilt rule matches, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Expand the product from A.

$$(x+1)(x-3)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

$$x^{2}-2x-3\neq x^{2}-2x+3$$

The constant term is $-3$, not $+3$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The axis is the midpoint of the roots.

$$x=\frac{-1+3}{2}$$

$$\frac{-1+3}{2}=1$$

$$1\neq 0$$

The axis is $x=1$, not $x=0$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Evaluate on the true axis $x=1$.

$$g(1)=1-2-3$$

$$1-2-3=-4$$

$$-4\neq -3$$

The vertex height is $-4$, not $-3$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The constant term is $g(0)$.

$$g(0)=(1)(-3)$$

$$(1)(-3)=-3$$

$$-3\neq 3$$

The constant term is $-3$, not $3$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

Axis $x=1$; vertex height $-4$.

tasks.title: Inverse line nested in a parabola
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=x-2$ (so $f^{-1}(x)=x+2$) and $g(x)=x^{2}-1$. Study $g(f^{-1}(x))$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The nested rule $g(f^{-1}(x))$ equals $(x+2)^{2}-1$.
Expanded, that nested rule is $x^{2}+4x+3$.
The nested rule vanishes at $x=-1$.
The nested rule vanishes at $x=-3$.
The nested rule is a parabola that opens upwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Substitute the inverse line into $g$.

$$f^{-1}(x)=x+2$$

$$g(f^{-1}(x))=(x+2)^{2}-1$$

The nested rule matches, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Expand the square and combine constants.

$$(x+2)^{2}-1=x^{2}+4x+4-1$$

$$x^{2}+4x+3$$

The expansion matches, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Substitute the named root candidate into the expansion.

$$(-1)^{2}+4(-1)+3=1-4+3$$

$$1-4+3=0$$

The nested rule vanishes at $x=-1$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The other factor of $x^{2}+4x+3=(x+1)(x+3)$ vanishes at $x=-3$.

$$(-3)^{2}+4(-3)+3=9-12+3$$

$$9-12+3=0$$

The nested rule vanishes at $x=-3$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

After expansion the leading coefficient is $1$.

$$a=1$$

$$a>0$$

The nested parabola opens upwards, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Substituting an inverse line shifts the roots of the parabola.

$$g(f^{-1}(x))=x^{2}+4x+3=(x+1)(x+3)$$

tasks.title: Repeated root
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=(x-2)^{2}$. Decide each claim. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph meets the horizontal axis at exactly one point.
The vertex lies on the horizontal axis.
The axis of symmetry is $x=3$.
Expanding gives $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+5$.
The discriminant of $g$ equals $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A square $(x-2)^{2}$ has a double root at $x=2$, hence a single meeting with the axis.

$$(x-2)^{2}=0$$

$$x=2$$

There is exactly one axis meeting, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

At the double root the height is $0$, so the vertex sits on the axis.

$$g(2)=(2-2)^{2}$$

$$g(2)=0$$

The vertex lies on the horizontal axis, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The axis is the vertical line through the repeated root.

$$x=2$$

$$2\neq 3$$

The axis is $x=2$, not $x=3$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Expand the square.

$$(x-2)^{2}=x^{2}-4x+4$$

$$4\neq 5$$

The constant term is $4$, not $5$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The discriminant of a repeated-root quadratic is zero.

$$\Delta=(-4)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 4$$

$$(-4)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 4=16-16$$

$$16-16=0$$

$$0\neq 1$$

The discriminant is $0$, not $1$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A double root is tangency with the axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+4\qquad\Delta=0$$

tasks.title: Symmetric table plus a fit test
tasks.context: The table samples an unknown rule $q$. No formula is printed. Two claims also offer candidate formulas to test against the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The table is symmetric about $x=2$.
The second differences are constant.
The candidate $q(x)=(x-2)^{2}+1$ matches every listed point.
The candidate $q(x)=|x-2|+1$ matches every listed point.
Extending the second-difference pattern gives $q(5)=8$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Read pairs equally far from $x=2$.

$$q(0)=q(4)$$

$$q(4)=5$$

$$q(1)=q(3)$$

$$q(3)=2$$

$$q(2)=1$$

The table is symmetric about $x=2$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Form first differences, then their gaps.

$$(-3,-1,1,3)$$

$$(2,2,2)$$

Second differences are constant, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Check each listed $x$ against the candidate.

$$(0-2)^{2}+1=5$$

$$(1-2)^{2}+1=2$$

$$(2-2)^{2}+1=1$$

$$(3-2)^{2}+1=2$$

$$(4-2)^{2}+1=5$$

Every listed point matches, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The absolute-value candidate already fails at the left endpoint.

$$|0-2|+1=3$$

$$3\neq 5$$

The candidate fails at $x=0$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

One more constant second difference $2$ lifts the last first difference from $3$ to $5$.

$$q(5)=q(4)+5$$

$$q(4)+5=5+5$$

$$5+5=10$$

$$10\neq 8$$

The extrapolated value is $10$, not $8$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$q(x)=(x-2)^{2}+1$$

Symmetric about $x=2$; second differences constantly $2$; $q(5)=10$.

tasks.title: Bridge arch described in words
tasks.context: A bridge arch is the part of $g(x)=4-(x-2)^{2}$ above the road $y=0$. A maintenance trolley follows the chord $f(x)=2-\frac12 x$ on the same interval. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The arch meets the road at $x=0$ and $x=4$.
The crown of the arch is at height $4$.
The trolley path has slope $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
At the crown abscissa the trolley is at height $1$.
The trolley path lies above the arch at $x=2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The arch meets the road where $g$ vanishes.

$$4-(x-2)^{2}=0$$

$$(x-2)^{2}=4$$

$$x=0,\; x$$

$$0,\; x=4$$

The arch meets the road at $x=0$ and $x=4$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The crown is the vertex, at $x=2$.

$$g(2)=4-(0)^{2}$$

$$4-(0)^{2}=4$$

The crown height is $4$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The slope of a line is the coefficient of $x$.

$$f(x)=2-\frac{1}{2}x$$

$$m=-\frac{1}{2}$$

The trolley path has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluate the trolley rule at the crown abscissa $x=2$.

$$f(2)=2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2$$

$$2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2=2-1$$

$$2-1=1$$

The trolley is at height $1$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Compare the two heights at $x=2$.

$$f(2)=1$$

$$g(2)=4$$

$$1<4$$

The trolley lies below the arch at $x=2$, not above it, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
$$g(x)=4-(x-2)^{2}\qquad f(x)=2-\frac{1}{2}x$$

Crown $(2,4)$; trolley height $1$ at the same abscissa.
